raw_text:
Here’s a concise, all-in-one summary of the complete 12-week program tailored for your 27-year-old beginner client training at home with just a yoga mat and a doorway pull-up bar. It combines strength, cardio, mobility, a weekly Saturday finisher, and a practical nutrition plan. The structure uses four main training days per week (A–D), with a progressive build across four phases (foundation, progression, strength, peak) and built-in deload/retrospective elements. I’ve included week-by-week outlines, exercise selections, sets/reps, tempo cues, and notes on recovery and progression. You can drop this into a calendar or hand it to the client as a one-page program.

Overall program design
- Training days: 4 main sessions per week (A Push, B Pull, C Lower, D Full Body). Optional mobility/cardio days and a dedicated Saturday finisher.
- Weekly rhythm: 1 push day, 1 pull day, 1 lower body day, 1 full-body/conditioning day; 1 dedicated mobility focus day or light cardio/rest as needed.
- Equipment: bodyweight, doorway pull-up bar, yoga mat; optional add-ons if/when available (dumbbells, kettlebell, resistance bands).
- Progression principle: increase reps toward target first, then use tempo, pauses, and leverage. Add volume gradually, then introduce modest loading via equipment if available.
- Recovery: warm-up 5–8 minutes, cool-down after sessions, 7–9 hours sleep, 2–3 L water, protein-focused nutrition (1.6–2.2 g/kg/day).

Phase 1: Foundation and technique (Weeks 1–3)
Goals: establish movement patterns, technique, and consistency; build confidence with bodyweight exercises.

Week 1
- Session A (Push)
  - Warm-up: 5–8 minutes dynamic
  - Push-ups from knees or incline: 3 x 8–10
  - Pike push-ups (or decline push-ups): 3 x 6–8
  - Plank: 3 x 20–30s
  - Shoulder taps: 3 x 8 per side
- Session B (Pull)
  - Inverted rows on doorway bar (feet on floor, angle): 3 x 6–8
  - Negative pull-ups or dead hangs: 3 x 4–6s
  - Supine glute bridge: 3 x 12
  - Side plank: 3 x 20–30s per side
- Session C (Lower)
  - Bodyweight squats: 3 x 10–12
  - Narrow split squats (chair): 3 x 8–10 per leg
  - Glute bridges: 3 x 12–15
  - Calf raises: 3 x 12–15
  - Bird-dog: 3 x 8 per side
- Session D (Full Body)
  - Mountain climbers: 3 x 20–30s
  - Push-up with knee drive: 3 x 6–8
  - Row hold/squeeze (doorway bar support): 3 x 20–30s
  - Dead bug: 3 x 8 per side
  - Core circuit: dead bug, side plank (2 rounds)

Week 2
- Similar to Week 1 with +1–2 reps where possible
- Emphasize tempo: 2–0–2 tempo on squats/push-ups; control the lowering phase

Week 3
- Push/pull emphasis with higher reps
  - Session A: Push-ups 3–4 x 9–12; incline as needed; planks 3 x 30–40s
  - Session B: Inverted rows 3–4 x 8–10; assisted negatives 3 x 5–6s
  - Session C: Squats 3 x 12–15; split squats 3 x 9–11 per leg
  - Session D: Full body circuit 3 rounds: Mtn climbers 30s, push-ups 8–10, inverted rows 8–10, glute bridges 15–20, dead bugs 10 per side

Phase 2: Progressive overload with tempo and paused reps (Weeks 4–6)
Goals: Increase push intensity and overall effort; introduce tempo, paused reps, and small loading options when possible.

Week 4
- Session A (Push)
  - Push-ups 3–4 x 8–12 (3–0–3 tempo; 1s pause bottom)
  - Pike push-ups or elevated-hand variations: 3 x 6–8
  - Plank variations: front 30–45s; side 20–30s
  - Isometric bottom hold: 2–3s x 3
  - Optional: light floor press with dumbbells if available: 3 x 6–8
- Session B (Pull)
  - Inverted rows 3–4 x 8–10
  - Negative pull-ups: 3 x 5–6s
  - Supine glute bridge 3 x 15
  - Core dead bug 3 x 10 per side
- Session C (Lower)
  - Slow tempo squats: 3–4 x 10–12, 3–0–3
  - Step-ups to chair: 3 x 8–10 per leg
  - Hip thrusts on mat: 3 x 12–15
  - Calf raises: 3 x 15–20
- Session D (Full Body)
  - Circuit: push-up 8–10, inverted row 8–10, split squat 8–10 per leg, glute bridge 15, hollow hold 3 x 20–30s

Week 5
- Increase total reps or add a set; maintain tempo
- If available, add light dumbbells for floor press or incline press (3–4 x 6–8)
- Core: add side planks 3 x 20–30s per side

Week 6
- Push-ups 4 x 9–12; mix incline/decline variations
- Inverted rows 4 x 8–10
- Lower: tempo squats 4 x 10 (3–0–3)
- Full body: 4 rounds of circuit with shorter rest (45–60s)

Phase 3: Strength emphasis with heavier sets (Weeks 7–9)
Goals: Move to lower reps with controlled eccentrics; build real pressing strength and pulling capacity.

Week 7
- Session A (Push)
  - Push-ups 4 x 6–8 with 3–0–3 tempo; add 1s pause at bottom if possible
  - Pike push-ups or straight-bar push-ups if available: 3 x 6–8
  - Core: front plank 3 x 45–60s
- Session B (Pull)
  - Inverted rows 4 x 6–8
  - Negative pull-ups 4 x 4–6s
  - Superman holds: 3 x 15
- Session C (Lower)
  - Goblet-like squat with arms forward (bodyweight): 4 x 8–10
  - Hip hinge (ROM) 4 x 8–10
  - Bulgarian split squat (chair): 3–4 x 6–8 per leg
- Session D (Full Body)
  - Circuit: push-up 6–8, inverted row 6–8, squat 8–10, glute bridge 12–15, plank 40–60s

Week 8
- Similar to Week 7; add 1–2 reps or another set as tolerable
- Encourage deeper ROM or slower tempo on key moves

Week 9
- Push/pull emphasis with preserved form
- Push-ups 4 x 6–8; add deficit or elevated hand variations if able
- Pull: 4 x 6–8 with top-position hold 1–2s when possible
- Lower: 4 x 8–10 squats; split squats 4 x 8 per leg
- Full body: 4 rounds; minimal rest

Phase 4: Peak strength and consolidation (Weeks 10–12)
Goals: Peak strength, slight taper, and testing readiness. Optional retest at Week 12.

Week 10
- Session A (Push)
  - Push-ups 4 x 6–8 with 2–0–2 tempo
  - Pike push-ups or elevated push-ups: 3 x 6–8
  - Hollow holds: 3 x 20–30s
- Session B (Pull)
  - Pull-ups/Negatives: 4 x 4–6s or 4 x max
  - Inverted rows: 4 x 6–8
- Session C (Lower)
  - Squats: 4 x 8–10 with full depth; tempo 2–0–2
  - Hip thrusts/bridge progression: 3–4 x 12–15
  - Calf raises: 4 x 15–20
- Session D (Full Body)
  - 4 rounds: push-up 6–8, row 6–8, squat 8–10, hinge 8–10, core 2 rounds

Week 11
- Deload-style: reduce volume ~40%; keep movement quality high
- Focus on mobility, technique, and light cardio if desired

Week 12
- Test week (optional)
  - Push-ups max reps in 60 seconds or 2–3 sets to failure
  - Inverted rows max reps in 60 seconds
  - Squats max reps in 60 seconds
  - Pull-up attempts (max or negatives)
- Decide follow-up plan: maintenance, or start Cycle 2 with increased baselines

Saturday Finisher Day (weekly, every Saturday)
- 20–25 minutes total
- Four circuits plus mobility/breathing finish
- Core + anti-rotation, metabolic burner, grip/pull-down ends, fun finishers
- Scales by ability (beginner to advanced)
- Space-friendly substitutions and optional equipment additions as available

Mobility Routine (integrated)
- Daily 8–12 minutes; 6–8 drills, 30–60s per drill
- Routine A/B/C/D options; rotate to cover shoulders/ thoracic spine/hips/ankles/spine/core
- Progress hold times every 2–3 weeks
- Use as warm-up, post-workout, or rest-day flow

Nutrition plan (starter framework)
- Protein: 1.6–2.2 g/kg bodyweight/day; distribute 25–40 g per meal
- Fat: ~0.8–1.0 g/kg/day
- Carbs: remaining calories after protein and fat
- Calorie target: start with maintenance (~2,400–2,700 kcal/day for many 27-year-olds) and +250 kcal/day if lean mass gain is desired
- Hydration: 2–3 L/day
- Post-workout: 20–40 g protein + 30–60 g carbs within 60–90 minutes
- Weekly tracking: weigh-in, adjust calories by +/− 200–300 kcal based on trend

Cardio plan (home-friendly)
- 2–3 cardio sessions/week; 15–30 minutes typical; 20–40 minutes on higher-energy weeks
- Formats: interval bodyweight cardio, tempo steady-state, bodyweight circuits, and low-impact options
- Progression: increase duration, rounds, or intensity in Phase 2–3
- Integration: avoid over-fatigue that could hinder lifting quality

Equipment purchases (optional, progressive)
- Start with a compact pair of dumbbells (e.g., 8–12 kg), or adjustable dumbbells
- Add a kettlebell (12–16 kg)
- Resistance bands with door anchor
- Optional: compact barbell with bumper plates later on
- Prioritize space-saving and cost-to-use efficiency; progress as client tolerates

Progress tracking and reassessment
- Weekly: track reps, sets, RPE, technique quality, and any pains
- Monthly: bodyweight and performance trend; adjust nutrition and volume if needed
- Phase transitions: ensure form remains solid; if any pain flares, revert to safer progression and revisit technique

What I can customize next
- If you share client’s current weight, height, lift maxes (e.g., push-ups max, pull-up ability), and preferred equipment/budget, I can:
  - Calculate precise macro targets and calorie targets
  - Produce a week-by-week calendar with exact daily sessions, tempo, and progression cues
  - Create a printable 1-page plan for the client and a separate trainer-facing sheet with notes
  - Build a tailored nutrition checklist, grocery list, and a 2-week re-evaluation plan

Would you like me to tailor the calendar to your client’s exact measurements, and generate a ready-to-print 12-week plan with daily sessions (A–D), nutrition targets, and the Saturday finisher as a one-page handout? If yes, share approximate bodyweight, height, typical weekly activity level, and any dietary preferences or constraints.

It’s divided into four 3-week blocks (mesocycles) with a deload and clear progression cues. I’ve included weekly session outlines, exercise selections, sets/reps, and notes on tempo, technique, recovery, and basic nutrition guidelines suitable for this setup.

Assumptions
- Week structure: 4 sessions per week (A, B, C, D). Optional 5th mobility/core or light cardio day is allowed if energy permits.
- Rest: 60–90 seconds between work sets for primary lifts; 30–60 seconds for accessory work.
- Progression: Increase reps toward target first, then intensity (tempo changes, adding pause reps, or increasing sets gradually) when target reps are reached.
- Equipment: Bodyweight, doorway pull-up bar, yoga mat. Modifications included for rows, push exercises, and leg work using leverage from the doorway and floor.
- Safety: Warm up before every session (5–8 minutes) and cool-down/stretch after.

Overall program structure
- Phase 1 (Weeks 1–3): Foundation and technique, develop movement patterns, build comfort with bodyweight strength.
- Phase 2 (Weeks 4–6): Progressive overload with higher effort, introduce slight difficulty via tempo and paused reps, start adding load via technique cues (negative reps, controlled eccentrics) and rep ranges.
- Phase 3 (Weeks 7–9): Strength emphasis with heavier sets, lower rep ranges, and more demanding variations.
- Phase 4 (Weeks 10–12): Peak strength focus, consolidation, and a mini deload at Week 10–11, culminating in a test/retesting movement at Week 12.

Weekly session framework
- Session A: Push emphasis (upper body push, core)
- Session B: Pull emphasis (upper body pull, posterior chain)
- Session C: Lower body emphasis (quad/hamstring/glute, core)
- Session D: Full body/conditioning and skill work (hybrid)
- Optional Mobility/Core days on off days or light cardio 15–30 minutes as needed.

Phase 1: Foundation and technique (Weeks 1–3)
Goals: Learn movement patterns; establish baseline strength; establish consistency.

Week 1
- Session A (Push)
  - Warm-up: 5–8 minutes (arm circles, scapular push-ups, inchworms, light glute bridges)
  - Push-ups from knees (or incline push-ups on a countertop/edge): 3 sets x 8–10 reps
  - Pike push-up progressions (or decline push-ups if possible): 3 x 6–8
  - Dumbbell? None available; use isometric holds
  - Plank: 3 x 20–30s
  - Shoulder taps (from push-up position): 3 x 8 per side
- Session B (Pull)
  - Warm-up: scapular activation, band-less rows? Use doorway bar
  - Inverted rows under doorway bar (feet on ground, body at angle): 3 x 6–8
  - Negative pull-ups (if able) or dead hangs: 3 x 4–6s hold x 3
  - Supine glute bridge with hamstring squeeze: 3 x 12
  - Side plank: 3 x 20–30s per side
- Session C (Lower)
  - Bodyweight squats: 3 x 10–12
  - Narrow split squats (bulgarian not possible; use a chair): 3 x 8–10 per leg
  - Glute bridges: 3 x 12–15
  - Calf raises: 3 x 12–15
  - Bird-dog: 3 x 8 per side
- Session D (Full Body)
  - Mountain climbers: 3 x 20–30s
  - Push-up with knee drive (or regular push-up if possible): 3 x 6–8
  - Row hold + squeeze (using doorway bar as support): 3 x 20–30s
  - Dead bug: 3 x 8 per side
  - Core circuit: dead bug, side plank (each side) 2 rounds

Week 2
- Repeat Week 1 but increase reps by 1–2 where comfortable; maintain technique.
- Emphasize tempo: control lowering phase (2–0–2 tempo) and pause 1–2 seconds at bottom for squats and push-ups.

Week 3
- Push/pull emphasis with increased reps:
  - Session A: Push-ups to 3 x 9–12; incline push-ups to failure if possible; planks 3 x 30–40s
  - Session B: Inverted rows 3 x 8–10; assisted pull-up negatives 3 x 5–6s
  - Session C: Squats 3 x 12–15; split squats 3 x 9–11 per leg
  - Session D: Full body circuit with longer sets (3 rounds): mountain climbers 30s, push-ups 8–10, inverted rows 8–10, glute bridges 15–20, dead bugs 10 per side

Phase 2: Progressive overload with tempo and paused reps (Weeks 4–6)
Goals: Increase intensity via tempo, pause reps, and increased leg/hip strength.

Week 4
- Session A (Push)
  - Push-ups: 3–4 x 8–12 (control, tempo 3–0–3; pause at bottom for 1s)
  - Pike to floor press progression: 3 x 6–8
  - Plank variations: front plank 3 x 30–45s; side planks 3 x 20–30s
  - Dips not available; skip or perform chair-assisted if available
- Session B (Pull)
  - Inverted rows: 3–4 x 8–10
  - Negative pull-ups: 3 x 5–6s
  - Supine glute bridge with hamstring squeeze: 3 x 15
  - Core: dead bug 3 x 10 per side
- Session C (Lower)
  - Slow tempo squats: 3–4 x 10–12 with 3–0–3 tempo
  - Step-ups to chair: 3 x 8–10 per leg
  - Hip thrusts on mat: 3 x 12–15
  - Calf raises: 3 x 15–20
- Session D (Full body)
  - Circuit: push-up 8–10, inverted row 8–10, split squat 8–10 per leg, glute bridge 15, hollow body hold 3 x 20–30s

Week 5
- Increase total reps by 10–15% or add a set to each routine where feasible.
- Emphasize paused reps and stricter form.
- Consider slightly elevated push-up progression (feet on floor if possible, otherwise continue incline).

Week 6
- Push-ups: 4 x 9–12; incline + decline variations mixed
- Inverted rows: 4 x 8–10
- Lower: tempo squats 4 x 10 with 3–0–3
- Full body: 4 rounds of circuit with reduced rest (45–60s)

Phase 3: Strength emphasis with heavier sets (Weeks 7–9)
Goals: Move toward lower reps with controlled eccentrics to build genuine strength.

Week 7
- Session A (Push)
  - Push-ups: 4 x 6–8 with tempo 3–0–3; add pause at bottom 1s if possible
  - Pike push-up progression or straight bar push-ups if available
  - Core: front plank 3 x 45–60s
- Session B (Pull)
  - Inverted rows: 4 x 6–8
  - Negative pull-ups (if possible): 4 x 4–6s
  - Superman holds: 3 x 15
- Session C (Lower)
  - Goblet-like squat with bodyweight: 4 x 8–10 (hold arms forward for balance)
  - Romanian hinge (hip hinge) without weight: 4 x 8–10
  - Bulgarian split squat using chair: 3–4 x 6–8 per leg
- Session D (Full body)
  - Circuit: push-up 6–8, inverted row 6–8, squat 8–10, glute bridge 12–15, plank 40–60s

Week 8
- Similar to Week 7 but increase reps slightly or add an extra set.
- Introduce a mild progression: increase range of motion where safe.

Week 9
- Push/pull emphasis with preserved form
- Push-ups 4 x 6–8; add deficit push-ups if possible (hands on a raised surface)
- Pull: 4 x 6–8 with held top position on pull-ups for 1–2s if achievable
- Lower: 4 x 8–10 for squats; split squats 4 x 8 per leg
- Full body: 4 rounds, minimal rest

Phase 4: Peak strength and consolidation (Weeks 10–12)
Goals: Consolidate gains; taper slightly to peak. Testing movement at Week 12 if client is comfortable.

Week 10
- Session A (Push)
  - Push-ups: 4 x 6–8 with max depth; tempo 2–0–2
  - Pike push-ups or elevated hand push-ups: 3 x 6–8
  - Core: hollow hold 3 x 20–30s
- Session B (Pull)
  - Pull-ups/Negative pull-ups: 4 x 4–6s or 4 x max reps
  - Inverted rows: 4 x 6–8
- Session C (Lower)
  - Squats: 4 x 8–10 with full depth; tempo 2–0–2
  - Hip thrusts/bridge progression: 3–4 x 12–15
  - Calf raises: 4 x 15–20
- Session D (Full body)
  - Circuit: push-up 6–8, row 6–8, squat 8–10, hinge 8–10, core 2 rounds

Week 11
- Deload style: reduce volume by ~40% but maintain technique; keep movements smooth
- Focus on mobility and form
- Light aerobic activity optional

Week 12
- Test week (optional): Reassess best indicator of progress
  - Push-ups max reps in 60 seconds, or 2–3 sets to failure
  - Inverted rows max reps in 60 seconds
  - Squats max reps in 60 seconds
  - Pull-up attempts if possible
- Based on test results, plan a maintenance approach or next cycle starting with Phase 1 again at a higher baseline.

Form cues and technique
- Push exercises: prioritize scapular retraction, tight core, neutral spine, elbows close to torso when appropriate (not flared).
- Pull exercises: keep shoulders down and back; avoid shrugging; use full range of motion where possible.
- Lower body: full hip hinge for posterior chain; chest up, knee tracking over toes; avoid knee collapse inward.

Great idea to add cardio that fits a small flat with minimal equipment. Here’s a home cardio plan that complements the 12-week strength program, requires no special gear, and can be scaled to energy levels and progression phases.

 Goals of the cardio component
- Improve cardiovascular health and work capacity
- Support recovery and fat management without compromising strength gains
- Provide variety and structure to keep motivation high

Structure and weekly layout
- Frequency: 2–3 cardio sessions per week (in addition to any optional mobility or light cardio days you already had)
- Duration: 15–30 minutes per session for most days; 20–40 minutes on higher-end weeks if energy permits
- Intensity: Use a mix of easy, moderate, and short high-intensity efforts. The emphasis should be on consistent effort and adherence, not maximum output
- Modes: Bodyweight intervals, low-impact options, and a few short cardio circuits that require only space

Cardio formats you can rotate through (choose 2–3 formats per week)
1) Interval bodyweight cardio (no equipment)
- 5-minute warm-up (dynamic moves: high knees, butt kicks, leg swings, arm circles)
- Intervals: 20–30 seconds hard pace / 40–60 seconds easy pace, repeat 8–12 rounds
- Exercises you can rotate:
  - High knees
  - Jumping jacks or low-impact step jacks
  - Mountain climbers
  - Burpees (low-impact version: step-out burpees or half-burpees)
  - Skaters (low-impact option: just step change)
- 5-minute cool-down and stretch

2) Tempo/steady-state cardio options
- 15–20 minutes continuous effort at a conversational but challenging pace
- Examples:
  - Marching or jogging in place with good posture
  - Rapid step-tounds (quick stepping side-to-side)
  - Staircase march on any internal stairs or a sturdy step (if available and safe)
- Focus on consistent breathing and posture

3) Cardio circuits for conditioning (no equipment)
- Perform 3–4 rounds with 30–45 seconds per exercise and 15–30 seconds rest between moves
  - Jump squats or bodyweight squats (low-impact: air squats)
  - Push-up to plank (push-up then rotate into side plank or a hold in plank)
  - Inchworm walkouts to push-up (or regular walking planks)
  - Lateral step-overs or side-to-side hops (or step touch)
  - Bicycle crunches or mountain climber variations

4) Low-impact options (great for active recovery days)
- Brisk walking around the home or balcony if space allows (even 10–15 minutes counts if done consistently)
- Gentle cycling on a stationary bike or a cautious brisk walk after meals (if outdoor access is limited)
- Gentle 10–15 minute yoga flow focusing on breathing and mobility can double as cardio if you maintain movement

Phase-aligned progression for cardio
- Phase 1 (Weeks 1–3): Start with 2 cardio sessions per week, 15–20 minutes each. Emphasize easy-to-moderate intensity and learn recovery breathing.
- Phase 2 (Weeks 4–6): Increase one session to 20–25 minutes or add 2–4 rounds to interval formats. Introduce one higher-intensity interval per session if capacity allows.
- Phase 3 (Weeks 7–9): Maintain 2–3 sessions, introduce one longer steady-state session (25–30 minutes) per week, keep intervals but with more rounds or longer hard intervals (e.g., 40 s hard / 60 s easy).
- Phase 4 (Weeks 10–12): Maintain 2–3 sessions; consider a “mini-test” cardio day (e.g., 20 minutes continuous at a comfortably hard pace) to monitor progress. If fatigued, dial back one session or reduce duration by 5–10 minutes.

Sample weekly cardio plan (example for Weeks 7–9)
- Monday: Strength Session A (Push) + 15–20 min interval cardio (8 rounds: 25s hard / 40s easy)
- Wednesday: Strength Session B (Pull) + 20–25 min steady-state cardio (tempo) or low-impact circuit
- Friday: Strength Session C (Lower) + 3 rounds of 6–8 minute cardio circuit (3 rounds of 45s on/15s off per move, total ~6–9 minutes active time, plus warm/cool)
- Optional Sunday: 15–20 minutes of brisk walking or light mobility-focused cardio

Safety and practicality tips
- Surface and space: Clear a safe area; keep corners free of furniture.
- Footwear: Wear supportive shoes if available; if not, ensure a flat surface and soft landing to reduce impact.
- Joint care: If any knee, ankle, or hip pain arises, switch to lower-impact options (marching in place, step-tause, walking, or 10–12 minutes of gentler circuits).
- Progression cues: If you can complete all intervals with good form and feel recovered, you can add a round or extend hard intervals by 5–10 seconds.
- Recovery: Hydrate after cardio; if you’re doing cardio the same day as heavy lifting, consider lowering the cardio duration slightly to avoid fatigue affecting lifting performance.

Tracking and integration with nutrition
- Keep cardio sessions as separate from lifting sessions when possible, or at least at a different time of day to optimize performance.
- If bodyweight management is a goal, track energy levels and adjust cardio volume if fatigue impacts lifts.
- Hydration and nutrition around cardio: a light snack with both protein and carbs before cardio can improve performance (e.g., a small yogurt, a banana with a little peanut butter).

- If ceiling height or space is restricted, favor low-impact intervals (marching, stepping, side steps) and longer steady-state sessions rather than explosive moves.

Here’s a practical, progressive buying plan that fits a small flat and a beginner-to-intermediate strength program.

Baseline approach (priority list)
- Start with core, space-efficient options that offer the best cost-to-use value and progressive overload capability.
- Aim to acquire 2–3 key pieces over time, rather than buying a full rack up front.

Recommended purchases in order

1) Adjustable dumbbells or fixed-weight dumbbells (space-efficient option)
- Pros: Versatile for presses, rows, goblet squats, Romanian deadlifts, lunges, and accessory work; easy to progress by small weight increments.
- Adjustable dumbbells: If budget allows, a compact set (e.g., adjustable from 5–25 kg per dumbbell) can replace a whole rack of plates. Look for smooth dial or quick-change collars, solid build, and reasonable balance.
- Fixed-weight option: A pair of moderate dumbbells (e.g., 10 kg each) plus a heavier pair later (e.g., 15–20 kg) works well for most beginners. You can also start with a single pair of moderate weight and use tempo, leverage, and reps to progress.

2) Kettlebell (one or two) as a supplement
- One adjustable kettlebell or a couple of fixed weights (e.g., 12–16 kg) is superb for hip hinges, goblet squats, carries, and dynamic movements.
- If choosing one: a 12–16 kg kettlebell covers many beginner-to-intermediate movements and travels well.

3) Resistance bands (various resistance)
- Lightweight, portable, and excellent for progressive overload in rows, face pulls, hip external rotation, glute work, and mobility work.
- Get a set: light, medium, and heavy bands (or a door-anchor kit) so you can tailor difficulty for push-ups, pull-aparts, banded squats, etc.

4) Optional: Olympic barbell with bumper plates (space and budget permitting)
- If he has long-term goals in strength and wants to run more advanced programs, a compact barbell (around 6–7 foot) with a small set of bumper plates (e.g., 5 kg, 10 kg, 15 kg) can be a great addition.
- However, for a 12-week home plan starting from bodyweight, this is optional. You can postpone until progress is consistently solid and space allows.

Recommended initial setup (gradual build, starting lightweight)
- Dumbbells: two adjustable 5–15 kg or two fixed weights (e.g., 8 kg and 12 kg). The idea is to be able to perform a goblet squat, row, press, and RDL with challenging loads.
- Kettlebell: 12–16 kg (or a single adjustable bell that covers that range).
- Resistance bands: set with light/medium/strong tones, plus a door anchor.
- Optional barbell: if space allows, a compact bar (6 ft) with a small bumper plate kit (5–10–15 kg).

Progression strategy with these tools
- Bodyweight to light weight: Use dumbbells/kettlebell to progress from bodyweight movements (push-ups, inverted rows) to weighted variants: goblet squats, dumbbell presses, bent-over rows, farmer’s walks.
- Tempo and reps: Before increasing weight, increase time under tension (slower tempo, paused reps) and/or add sets/reps. For example, move from 3x8 to 4x8 with a 3–0–3 tempo.
- Unilateral work: Use one heavier dumbbell for single-arm rows, goblet squats, and single-leg supported moves to build balance and core stability.
- Accessory lifts: Use bands for face pulls, pull-aparts, triceps pushdowns, and hip extensions to complement main lifts.

Budget-conscious packing list (low upfront cost)
- A pair of adjustable dumbbells (or two mid-weight fixed dumbbells, e.g., 8 kg and 12 kg)
- A 12–16 kg kettlebell (or a single adjustable)
- A set of resistance bands (light, medium, heavy) with door anchor
- Optional: a compact Olympic barbell kit with a couple bumper plates if future progressions demand it

Key considerations for choosing gear
- Space: Measure the room where he will train. Choose compact dumbbells or an adjustable set that minimizes clutter.
- Build quality: Look for durable handles, good knurling (if using barbells/dumbbells), and sturdy locking mechanisms on adjustable sets.
- Progression range: Ensure the selected weights offer meaningful jumps. If increments are too large (e.g., jumps of 5–10 kg where your client stalls), bands and tempo are a good bridge.
- Safety: Enforce proper form with any added resistance. Start lighter and progress gradually to avoid joint strain.

This focuses on the pushing movements (Session A) and how to push the effort safely using tempo, paused reps, increased volume, and slight loading options that don’t require heavy equipment.

Goals for Push in Phase 2 (Weeks 4–6)
- Elevate effort on pressing patterns without sacrificing form.
- Introduce controlled eccentrics and pauses to build strength.
- Increase total volume and/or difficulty in push movements while maintaining technique.
- Keep pulling and lower-body work balanced to prevent imbalances.

Phase 2 push plan: structure and progression
- Weekly structure (for Weeks 4–6): 2 push-focused sessions per week (Session A in your plan), plus one lighter push session if you’re using a 4-day scheme.
- Primary mechanisms to increase push intensity:
  1) Tempo and pauses: slower eccentric, pausable bottom, and controlled concentric.
  2) Increased total volume: add an extra set or a higher rep range within target window.
  3) Progressions in leverage: move from incline to floor progression, or from knees to toes push-ups as technique allows.
  4) Short isometric holds: bottom-position holds to boost time under tension.
  5) Small load tricks via tempo and serviceable variations (no heavy external load required).

Phase 2 push-specific progression plan (Weeks 4–6)

Week 4
- Session A (Push)
  - Push-ups (on knees or incline as needed): 3–4 sets x 8–12 reps
  - Tempo push-ups (3-0-3; emphasis on slow descent, 1s pause at bottom, controlled ascent): 3–4 x 6–8
  - Pike push-up progression (or elevated hand push-ups if available): 3 x 6–8
  - Isometric bottom hold: push-up position hold at bottom for 2–3 seconds x 3 sets
  - Core: front plank 3 x 30–45s
- Optional add-on (if ready and equipment allows): Single-arm floor press with dumbbell if available, 3 x 6–8 per arm (substitute if you’ve got light dumbbells; otherwise skip)

Week 5
- Session A (Push)
  - Push-ups: 4 x 8–12 (keep tempo 3-0-3)
  - Pike push-ups or elevated hand push-ups: 3 x 6–8
  - Decline to incline progression: if you can do flat push-ups with solid form, add a slight elevation for the bottom of the movement? If not, keep with current progression.
  - Bottom-strike pause push-ups: 3 x 2–3 reps at bottom with 2-second hold
  - Core: side planks 3 x 20–30s per side

Week 6
- Session A (Push)
  - Push-ups: 4 x 9–12 with controlled tempo; aim to reach upper end with solid form
  - Decline push-ups (feet elevated on a stable chair/step): 3 x 6–8
  - Floor press progression (if dumbbells available): 3 x 8–10 with a controlled tempo
  - Isometric mid-range hold: hold at 45–60 degrees angle (mid-push position) for 15–20s x 3 sets
  - Core: carry-over: hollow body holds 3 x 20–30s

Key tempo cues and technique tips for Phase 2 push
- Tempo: 3-0-3 for most sets in Weeks 4–6. If you can do 4-second eccentric while maintaining control, and a deliberate 1–2 second pause at the bottom for some reps, that’s ideal.
- Elbow position: keep elbows slightly tucked (about 45 degrees from the torso) to protect the shoulders. Don’t flare for too long.
- Scapular stability: protract and retract the shoulder blades subtly to maintain a solid base; avoid sagging hips or flaring ribs.
- Range of motion: aim for full ROM where possible (chest to touch the floor in push-ups), but respect range if mobility is limiting. Use incline to gradually progress to full push-ups.
- Breathing: exhale on the push, inhale on the way down.

Load and progression logic (without heavy equipment)
- If you can’t add external weight, progress by:
  - Increasing reps within the same set range (e.g., 8–12 to 9–12)
  - Adding a paused rep or pause-at-bottom rep
  - Extending the total number of sets from 3 to 4
  - Switching from incline to floor push-ups as technique allows
- If you have access to light weights (dumbbells) or bands:
  - Introduce light dumbbell floor press or incline press: 3–4 x 6–8
  - Use a tempo that matches the plan (2–0–2 to 3–0–3)
  - For dumbbell push-ups, perform with hands on dumbbells to increase ROM and add load

Reassessment plan during Phase 2
- Weekly checks: ensure reps are achieved with good form and no shoulder pain.
- If shoulders feel unstable or pain arises, revert to safer variations (incline push-ups, isometric holds, reduce tempo) and focus on scapular control.
- At the end of Week 6, you should be able to do near-maximum push-ups for a given rep range with proper technique; this sets a baseline for Phase 3 (strength emphasis with heavier loads and lower reps).

Integration with other phases
- Keep in balance: Phase 2 push intensity increases should be mirrored by a stable or increased pull and leg workload to prevent imbalances and overreaching fatigue.
- Ensure at least one rest day after push-focused workouts if you’re feeling fatigued; otherwise, your next lower-body or pull session can be adjusted in volume.

Optional substitutions and safety
- If the door pull-up bar creates grip discomfort during push movements, adjust hand position or switch to incline push-ups to reduce load on wrists.
- If any pain arises in the wrists or shoulders, switch to wrist-friendly variations like wall slides for warm-up, or push-ups on fists/knuckles to reduce angle.

Structure

Mobility routines (choose 1 short routine per day or rotate through them)

Routine A: Shoulders, thoracic spine, and hips (great as a daily warm-up)
- Cat-Cow dynamic spine mobility: 1 minute
- Thoracic spine windscreens (thread the needle with a reach): 1 minute
- Doorway pec/shoulder opener: 2 x 30–45s per side (stand in doorway, step through to feel stretch across chest and front shoulder)
- Thread-the-needle thoracic rotation in quadruped: 2 rounds per side, 30–45s
- Hip flexor stretch in lunge: 2 x 30–45s per side
- Open/close hips (90/90 position): 2 rounds per side, 30s hold each, slow transitions
- Shoulder dislocations with a towel or band: 2 x 12 reps

Routine B: Ankles, knees, hips, and hips-to-back
- Ankle circles and alphabet drills: 1 minute total
- Deep squat mobility with hold: 2 rounds x 30–45s at bottom, aiming for elbows inside knees
- Hip hinges (pelvic tilts and hip hinge with slight knee bend): 2 x 30s
- Quadruped rock-back (creep back to sit bones): 2 rounds x 30–40s
- World's greatest stretch (couch/step variation if space limited): 1–2 rounds per side, 30–45s
- Couch stretch (if possible): 1–2 x 30–60s per side

Routine C: Spine, core, and ribcage
- Dead bug variations with thoracic reach: 2 rounds x 30–45s
- Standing thoracic rotation with arms hugged (or band): 2 x 30–45s per side
- Paloff presses or anti-rotation hold (use resistance band or doorway bar if available): 2 x 20–30s per side
- Swiss ball or wedge hip flexor/quad stretch if you have a small cushion: 2 x 30s per side
- Hollow body mobility drill: 2 x 30–45s

Routine D: Full-body flow (active mobility circuit)
- Dynamic leg swings front-to-back and side-to-side: 1 minute total
- Gate stretch with lateral lunge to reach: 2 rounds per side, 30s
- Spinal waves on mat (seated/child’s pose to reach overhead): 2 rounds x 30s
- Inchworm with push-up (or walking plank) to finish: 2 rounds x 30–45s
- Breathing and bracing drill: 2 rounds x 60s (box breathing 4s in, 4s hold, 4s out, 4s hold)

Weekly progression tips
- Weeks 1–3: Keep each pose gentle; focus on breathing, comfort, and posture alignment. Hold at the end of each stretch for 30–45 seconds.
- Weeks 4–6: Increase hold times to 45–60 seconds where feasible; add a 5–10 second deeper hold on the key stretches (hip flexors, thoracic spine).
- Weeks 7–9: Introduce a slow 1–2 second descent into deeper ranges (e.g., deeper squat hold, deeper couch stretch). Add light activation pauses (isometric holds) to improve neuromuscular awareness.
- Weeks 10–12: Flow with more smooth transitions between poses; consider adding a short 3–5 minute flow as a finisher on rest days or after workouts.

Key mobility targets aligned to the program
- Shoulders: improve overhead stability and reduce shoulder impingement risk for push movements.
- Thoracic spine: improve rotation and extension to support pulling and pressing mechanics.
- Hips and ankles: ensure deep squats and lunges are comfortable, reduce knee valgus risk, and support hinge patterns.
- Core: maintain solid trunk bracing and reduce excessive lumbar movement during lifts.
- Breathing: emphasize nasal/belly breathing during holds to improve recovery and parasympathetic activation.

Scheduling suggestions
- Pre-workout option: 6–8 minutes focusing on mobility that targets the day’s tissue areas (example: Routine A).
- Post-workout option: 6–8 minutes focusing on lower body and spine (Routine B or C).
- Rest day option: a light 8–12 minute mobility flow (combine Routines A–D into a gentle flow).

Printable plan example (starter week)

- Wednesday: Routine B (lower/hips)

- Saturday: Saturday Finisher Day (optional light mobility circuit or 5–10 minutes of breathing work)
- Sunday: Mobility/Recovery optional

Equipment considerations
- If you have a doorway pull-up bar: use it for scapular retraction pulls and light isometric hangs during Routine C as a gentle activation exercise.
- A yoga mat is great for floor-based stretches and mobility drills; a small cushion or towel can help with couch stretch or knee comfort.

Overall program design
- Training days: 4 main sessions per week (A Push, B Pull, C Lower, D Full Body). Optional mobility/cardio days and a dedicated Saturday finisher.
- Weekly rhythm: 1 push day, 1 pull day, 1 lower body day, 1 full-body/conditioning day; 1 dedicated mobility focus day or light cardio/rest as needed.
- Equipment: bodyweight, doorway pull-up bar, yoga mat; optional add-ons if/when available (dumbbells, kettlebell, resistance bands).
- Progression principle: increase reps toward target first, then use tempo, pauses, and leverage. Add volume gradually, then introduce modest loading via equipment if available.
- Recovery: warm-up 5–8 minutes, cool-down after sessions, 7–9 hours sleep, 2–3 L water, protein-focused nutrition (1.6–2.2 g/kg/day).

Phase 1: Foundation and technique (Weeks 1–3)
Goals: establish movement patterns, technique, and consistency; build confidence with bodyweight exercises.

Week 1
- Session A (Push)
  - Warm-up: 5–8 minutes dynamic
  - Push-ups from knees or incline: 3 x 8–10
  - Pike push-ups (or decline push-ups): 3 x 6–8
  - Plank: 3 x 20–30s
  - Shoulder taps: 3 x 8 per side
- Session B (Pull)
  - Inverted rows on doorway bar (feet on floor, angle): 3 x 6–8
  - Negative pull-ups or dead hangs: 3 x 4–6s
  - Supine glute bridge: 3 x 12
  - Side plank: 3 x 20–30s per side
- Session C (Lower)
  - Bodyweight squats: 3 x 10–12
  - Narrow split squats (chair): 3 x 8–10 per leg
  - Glute bridges: 3 x 12–15
  - Calf raises: 3 x 12–15
  - Bird-dog: 3 x 8 per side
- Session D (Full Body)
  - Mountain climbers: 3 x 20–30s
  - Push-up with knee drive: 3 x 6–8
  - Row hold/squeeze (doorway bar support): 3 x 20–30s
  - Dead bug: 3 x 8 per side
  - Core circuit: dead bug, side plank (2 rounds)

Week 2
- Similar to Week 1 with +1–2 reps where possible
- Emphasize tempo: 2–0–2 tempo on squats/push-ups; control the lowering phase

Week 3
- Push/pull emphasis with higher reps
  - Session A: Push-ups 3–4 x 9–12; incline as needed; planks 3 x 30–40s
  - Session B: Inverted rows 3–4 x 8–10; assisted negatives 3 x 5–6s
  - Session C: Squats 3 x 12–15; split squats 3 x 9–11 per leg

Week 4
